16.3 Nested transactions 
Nested transactions extend the above transaction model by allowing transactions to be 
composed of other transactions. Thus several transactions may be started from within a 
transaction, allowing transactions to be re garded as modules that can be co mposed as 
required.
The outer most transaction in a set of nested transactions is called the top-level
transaction. Transactions other than the top-level transaction are called subtransactions.
For e xample, in Fi gure 16.13, T is a top-level transaction that starts a pair of 
subtransactions, T1 and T2. The subtransaction T1 starts its own pair of subtransactions, 
T11 and T22. Also, subtransaction T2 starts its own subtransaction, T21, which starts 
another subtransaction, T211.
A subtransaction appears ato mic to its parent with respect to transaction failures 
and to concurrent access. Subtransactions at the sa me level, such as T1 and T2, can run 
concurrently, but their access to co mmon ob jects is serialized � for e xample, b y the 
locking scheme described in Section 16.4. Each subtransaction can fail independently of 
its parent and of the other subtransactions. When a subtransaction aborts, the parent 
transaction can sometimes choose an alternative subtransaction to complete its task. For 
example, a transaction to deliver a mail message to a list of recipients could be structured 
as a set of subtransactions, each of which delivers the message to one of the recipients. 
If one or more of the subtransactions fails, the parent transaction could record the fact 
and then co mmit, with the result that all the successful child transactions co mmit. It 
could then start another transaction to atte mpt to redeliver the messages that were not 
sent the first time.

When we need to distin guish our ori ginal form of transaction fro m nested ones, 
we use the term flat transaction. It is flat because all of its work is done at the same level 
between an openTransaction and a commit or abort, and it is not possible to commit or 
abort parts of it. Nested transactions have the following main advantages:
1. Subtransactions at one level (and their descendants) may run concurrentl y with 
other subtransactions at the same level in the hierarchy. This can allow additional 
concurrency in a transaction. When subtransactions run in different servers, the y 
can wor k in parallel. For e xample, consider the branchTotal operation in our 
banking example. It can be implemented by invoking getBalance at every account 
in the branch. Now each of these invocations may be perfor med as a 
subtransaction, in which case they can be performed concurrently. Since each one 
applies to a different account, there will be no conflictin g operations a mong the 
subtransactions.

16.3 Nested transactions 
Nested transactions extend the above transaction model by allowing transactions to be 
composed of other transactions. Thus several transactions may be started from within a 
transaction, allowing transactions to be re garded as modules that can be co mposed as 
required.
The outer most transaction in a set of nested transactions is called the toplevel
transaction. Transactions other than the toplevel transaction are called subtransactions.
For e xample, in Fi gure 16.13, T is a toplevel transaction that starts a pair of 
subtransactions, T1 and T2. The subtransaction T1 starts its own pair of subtransactions, 
T11 and T22. Also, subtransaction T2 starts its own subtransaction, T21, which starts 
another subtransaction, T211.
A subtransaction appears ato mic to its parent with respect to transaction failures 
and to concurrent access. Subtransactions at the sa me level, such as T1 and T2, can run 
concurrently, but their access to co mmon ob jects is serialized � for e xample, b y the 
locking scheme described in Section 16.4. Each subtransaction can fail independently of 
its parent and of the other subtransactions. When a subtransaction aborts, the parent 
transaction can sometimes choose an alternative subtransaction to complete its task. For 
example, a transaction to deliver a mail message to a list of recipients could be structured 
as a set of subtransactions, each of which delivers the message to one of the recipients. 
If one or more of the subtransactions fails, the parent transaction could record the fact 
and then co mmit, with the result that all the successful child transactions co mmit. It 
could then start another transaction to atte mpt to redeliver the messages that were not 
sent the first time.

 PAGE 709 
Figure 16.13 Nested transactions
T  : toplevel transaction
T1 = openSubTransaction T2 = openSubTransaction
openSubTransaction openSubTransactionopenSubTransaction
openSubTransaction
T1 : T2 :
T11 : T12 :

SECTION 16.3 NESTED TRANSACTIONS 691
When we need to distin guish our ori ginal form of transaction fro m nested ones, 
we use the term flat transaction. It is flat because all of its work is done at the same level 
between an openTransaction and a commit or abort, and it is not possible to commit or 
abort parts of it. Nested transactions have the following main advantages:
1. Subtransactions at one level (and their descendants) may run concurrentl y with 
other subtransactions at the same level in the hierarchy. This can allow additional 
concurrency in a transaction. When subtransactions run in different servers, the y 
can wor k in parallel. For e xample, consider the branchTotal operation in our 
banking example. It can be implemented by invoking getBalance at every account 
in the branch. Now each of these invocations may be perfor med as a 
subtransaction, in which case they can be performed concurrently. Since each one 
applies to a different account, there will be no conflictin g operations a mong the 
subtransactions. 
2. Subtransactions can co mmit or abort independentl y. In comparison with a single 
transaction, a set of nested subtransactions is potentiall y more robust. The above 
example of deliverin g mail shows that this is so � with a flat transaction, one 
transaction failure would cause the whole transaction to be restarted. In fact, a 
parent can decide on different actions accordin g to whether a subtransaction has 
aborted or not.
The rules for committing of nested transactions are rather subtle:
 A transaction may co mmit or abort onl y after its child transactions have 
completed.
 When a subtransaction co mpletes, it makes an independent decision either to 
commit provisionally or to abort. Its decision to abort is final.
 When a parent aborts, all of its subtransactions are aborted. For e xample, if T2
aborts then T21 and T211 must also abort, even though they may have provisionally 
committed.
 When a subtransaction aborts, the parent can decide whether to abort or not. In our 
example, T decides to commit although T2 has aborted.

 PAGE 710 
692 CHAPTER 16  TRANSACTIONS AND CONCURRENCY CONTROL
 If the toplevel transaction co mmits, then all of the subtransactions that have 
provisionally committed can commit too, provided that none of their ancestors has 
aborted. In our e xample, T's commitment allows T1, T11 and T12 to commit, but 
not T21 and T211 since their parent, T2, aborted. Note that the effects of a 
subtransaction are not permanent until the toplevel transaction commits. 
In some cases, the toplevel transaction may decide to abort because one or more of its 
subtransactions have aborted. As an e xample, consider the followin g Transfer
transaction: 
Transfer $100 from B to A
a.deposit(100)
b.withdraw(100)
This can be structured as a pair of subtransactions, one for the withdraw operation and 
the other for deposit. When the two subtransactions both co mmit, the Transfer
transaction can also co mmit. Suppose that a withdraw subtransaction aborts whenever 
an account is overdrawn. Now consider the case when the withdraw subtransaction 
aborts and the deposit subtransaction co mmits � and recall that the co mmitment of a 
child transaction is conditional on the parent transaction co mmitting. We presume that 
the toplevel ( Transfer) transaction will decide to abort. The abortin g of the parent 
transaction causes the subtransactions to abort � so the deposit transaction is aborted and 
all its effects are undone.
The COR BA Ob ject Transaction Service supports both flat and nested 
transactions. Nested transactions are particularl y useful in distributed s ystems because 
child transactions may be run concurrentl y in different servers. We return to this issue

transaction can sometimes choose an alternative subtransaction to complete its task. For 
example, a transaction to deliver a mail message to a list of recipients could be structured 
as a set of subtransactions, each of which delivers the message to one of the recipients.

and then co mmit, with the result that all the successful child transactions co mmit. It

    lines = text.split('\n')
    result = []

    while i < len(lines):

        if i + 1 < len(lines):

            # If line ends with hyphen, remove hyphen and join
            if line.rstrip().endswith('-') and next_line.strip() and not next_line.strip()[0].isupper():

                result.append(fixed)

            elif line.strip() and next_line.strip() and not line.rstrip().endswith(('.', '!', '?', ':', ';', ',', ')')) and next_line.strip()[0].islower():

# 16.3 Nested transactions

16.3 Nested transactions 
Nested transactions extend the above transaction model by allowing transactions to be composed of other transactions. Thus several transactions may be started from within a 
transaction, allowing transactions to be re garded as modules that can be co mposed as required.
The outer most transaction in a set of nested transactions is called the top-level transaction. Transactions other than the top-level transaction are called subtransactions.
For e xample, in Fi gure 16.13, T is a top-level transaction that starts a pair of subtransactions, T1 and T2. The subtransaction T1 starts its own pair of subtransactions, 
T11 and T22. Also, subtransaction T2 starts its own subtransaction, T21, which starts another subtransaction, T211.
A subtransaction appears ato mic to its parent with respect to transaction failures and to concurrent access. Subtransactions at the sa me level, such as T1 and T2, can run 
concurrently, but their access to co mmon ob jects is serialized â€“ for e xample, b y the locking scheme described in Section 16.4. Each subtransaction can fail independently of 
its parent and of the other subtransactions. When a subtransaction aborts, the parent transaction can sometimes choose an alternative subtransaction to complete its task. For 
example, a transaction to deliver a mail message to a list of recipients could be structured as a set of subtransactions, each of which delivers the message to one of the recipients. 
If one or more of the subtransactions fails, the parent transaction could record the fact and then co mmit, with the result that all the successful child transactions co mmit. It 
could then start another transaction to atte mpt to redeliver the messages that were not sent the first time.

content.text:
# 16.3 Nested transactions 
Nested transactions extend the above transaction model by allowing transactions to be composed of other transactions. Thus several transactions may be started from within a 
transaction, allowing transactions to be regarded as modules that can be composed as required.
The outer most transaction in a set of nested transactions is called the top-level transaction. Transactions other than the top-level transaction are called subtransactions.
For example, in Figure 16.13, T is a top-level transaction that starts a pair of subtransactions, T1 and T2. The subtransaction T1 starts its own pair of subtransactions, 
T11 and T22. Also, subtransaction T2 starts its own subtransaction, T21, which starts another subtransaction, T211.
A subtransaction appears atomic to its parent with respect to transaction failures and to concurrent access. Subtransactions at the same level, such as T1 and T2, can run 
concurrently, but their access to common objects is serialized – for example, by the locking scheme described in Section 16.4. Each subtransaction can fail independently of 
its parent and of the other subtransactions. When a subtransaction aborts, the parent transaction can sometimes choose an alternative subtransaction to complete its task. For 
example, a transaction to deliver a mail message to a list of recipients could be structured as a set of subtransactions, each of which delivers the message to one of the recipients.

In backward validation, the read set of the transaction being validated is compared with the write sets of other transactions that have already committed. Therefore, the only 
way to resolve any conflicts is to abort the transaction that is undergoing validation. 
In bac kward validation, transactions that have no read operations (only write operations) need not be checked.
Optimistic concurrency control with bac kward validation requires that the write sets of old committed versions of objects correspondin g to recentl y committed

boolean valid = true;
for (int Tid = active1; Tid <= activeN; Tid++){ if (write set of Tv intersects read set of Tid) valid = false;
}

 Defer the validation until a later ti me when the conflicting transactions have finished. However, there is no guarantee that the transaction bein g validated will 
fare any better in the future. There is alwa ys the chance that further conflicting active transactions may start before the validation is achieved.
 Abort all the conflicting active transactions and commit the transaction bein g validated.

content.text:
# 16.3 Transacciones anidadas
Transacciones anidadas extend the above transaction model by allowing transactions to be composed of other transactions. Thus several transactions may be started from within a
transaction, allowing transactions to be regarded as modules that can be composed as required.
The outer most transaction in a set of transacciones anidadas is called the transacción de nivel superior. Transactions other than the transacción de nivel superior are called subtransaccións.
For example, in Figure 16.13, T is a transacción de nivel superior that starts a pair of subtransaccións, T1 and T2. The subtransacción T1 starts its own pair of subtransaccións,
T11 and T22. Also, subtransacción T2 starts its own subtransacción, T21, which starts another subtransacción, T211.
A subtransacción appears atomic to its parent with respect to transaction failures and to concurrent access. Subtransactions at the same level, such as T1 and T2, can run
concurrently, but their access to common objects is serialized – for example, by the bloqueoing scheme described in Section 16.4. Each subtransacción can fail independently of
its parent and of the other subtransaccións. When a subtransacción aborts, the parent transaction can sometimes choose an alternative subtransacción to complete its task. For
example, a transaction to deliver a mail message to a list of recipients could be structured as a set of subtransaccións, each of which delivers the message to one of the recipients.
If one or more of the subtransaccións fails, the parent transaction could record the fact and then commit, with the result that all the successful child transactions commit. It
could then start another transaction to attempt to redeliver the messages that were not sent the first time.

Figure 16.13 Transacciones anidadas
T  : transacción de nivel superior

content.text:
Por ejemplo, en Figura 16.13, T es una transacción de nivel superior que inicia a pair of subtransacciones, T1 and T2. The subtransacción T1 inicia su propio par de subtransacciones,
T11 and T22. Además, la subtransacción T2 starts its own subtransacción, T21, que inicia otra subtransacción, T211.
Una subtransacción aparece atómica to its parent with respect to fallos de transacción and to acceso concurrente. Subtransaccións at the same level, such as T1 and T2, can run
concurrently, but their access to objetos comunes is serializado – por ejemplo, mediante el esquema de bloqueo descrito en la Sección 16.4. Cada subtransacción puede fallar de forma independiente of
its parent and of the other subtransacciones. When a subtransacción abortars, the parent transacción can sometimes choose una subtransacción alternativa para completar su tarea. For
example, a transacción to deliver a mail message to a lista de destinatarios could be estructurada como un conjunto de subtransacciones, cada una de las cuales entrega el mensaje to one of the recipients.
If una o más subtransacciones fallan, the parent transacción could record the fact and then confirmar, with the result that all the successful child transaccións confirmar. It
could then start another transacción para intentar reenviar the messages that were not sent the first time.

content.text:
# 16.3 Transacciones anidadas
Las transacciones anidadas extienden el modelo de transacciones anterior permitiendo que las transacciones se compongan de otras transacciones. Así, varias transacciones pueden iniciarse desde dentro de una
transacción, lo que permite que las transacciones se consideren módulos que pueden componerse según sea necesario.
La transacción más externa transacción en un conjunto de transacciones anidadas se denomina transacción de nivel superior. Las transacciones distintas de the transacción de nivel superior se denominan subtransacciones.
Por ejemplo, en Figura 16.13, T es una transacción de nivel superior que inicia un par de subtransacciones, T1 y T2. The subtransacción T1 inicia su propio par de subtransacciones,
T11 y T22. Además, la subtransacción T2 inicia su propia subtransacción, T21, que inicia otra subtransacción, T211.
Una subtransacción aparece atómica a su padre con respecto a fallos de transacción y al acceso concurrente. Las subtransacciones del mismo nivel, such as T1 y T2, can run
concurrentemente, pero su acceso a los objetos comunes está serializado – por ejemplo, mediante el esquema de bloqueo descrito en la Sección 16.4. Cada subtransacción puede fallar de forma independiente de
its parent y de las demás subtransacciones. Cuando una subtransacción aborta, la transacción padre puede elegir una subtransacción alternativa para completar su tarea. For
example, una transacción para entregar un mensaje de correo a una lista de destinatarios podría estructurarse como un conjunto de subtransacciones, cada una de las cuales entrega el mensaje a uno de los destinatarios.
Si una o más subtransacciones fallan, la transacción padre could record the fact and then confirmar, with the result that todas las transacciones hijas exitosas confirman. It
could then start another transacción para intentar reenviar los mensajes que no se enviaron la primera vez.

Figura 16.13 Transacciones anidadas
T  : transacción de nivel superior
T1 = openSubTransacción T2 = openSubTransacción openSubTransacción openSubTransacciónopenSubTransacción
openSubTransacción
T1 : T2 :
T11 : T12 :
T211 :
T21 :
provisional confirmar provisional confirmar
abortar provisional confirmarprovisional confirmar
provisional confirmar confirmar

When we need to distinguish our original form of transacción fro m nested ones,
we use the term transacción plana. Es plana porque todo su trabajo se realiza al mismo nivel between an openTransacción and a confirmar or abortar, and it is not possible to confirmar or
abortar parts of it. Transacciones anidadas have the following main advantages:
1. Subtransaccións at one level (and their descendants) may run concurrently with other subtransacciones at the same level in the hierarchy. This can allow additional
concurrency in a transacción. When subtransacciones run in different servers, the y can work in parallel. For example, consider the branchTotal operation in our
banking example. It can be implemented by invoking getBalance at every account in the branch. Now each of these invocations may be performed as a
subtransacción, in which case they can be performed concurrently. Since each one applies to a different account, there will be no conflicting operations a mong the
subtransacciones.
2. Subtransaccións can confirmar or abortar independently. In comparison with a single transacción, a set of nested subtransacciones is potentially more robust. The above
example of delivering mail shows that this is so – with a transacción plana, one transacción failure would cause the whole transacción to be restarted. In fact, a
parent can decide on different actions accordin g to whether a subtransacción has abortared or not.
The rules for confirmarting of transacciones anidadas are rather subtle:
 A transacción may confirmar or abortar only after its child transaccións have completed.
 When a subtransacción completes, it makes an independent decision either to confirmar provisionally or to abortar. Its decision to abortar is final.
 When a parent abortars, all of its subtransacciones are abortared. For example, if T2 abortars then T21 and T211 must also abortar, even though they may have provisionally
confirmarted.
 Cuando una subtransacción aborta, the parent can decide whether to abortar or not. In our example, T decides to confirmar although T2 has abortared.

--- PAGE 710 --692
 If the transacción de nivel superior confirmars, then all of the subtransacciones that have provisionally confirmarted can confirmar too, provided that none of their ancestors has
abortared. In our example, T's confirmarment allows T1, T11 and T12 to confirmar, but not T21 and T211 since their parent, T2, abortared. Note that the effects of a
subtransacción are not permanent until the transacción de nivel superior confirmars.
In some cases, the transacción de nivel superior may decide to abortar because one or more of its subtransacciones have abortared. As an example, consider the following Transfer
transacción:
Transfer $100 from B to A a.deposit(100)
b.withdraw(100)
This can be structured as un par de subtransacciones, one for the withdraw operation and the other for deposit. When the two subtransacciones both confirmar, the Transfer
transacción can also confirmar. Suppose that a withdraw subtransacción abortars whenever an account is overdrawn. Now consider the case when the withdraw subtransacción
abortars and the deposit subtransacción confirmars – and recall that the confirmarment of a child transacción is conditional on la transacción padre confirmarting. We presume that
the nivel superior ( Transfer) transacción will decide to abortar. The abortaring of la transacción padre causes the subtransacciones to abortar – so the deposit transacción is abortared and
all its effects are undone.
The COR BA Ob ject Transacción Service supports both flat and transacciones anidadas. Transacciones anidadas are particularly useful in distributed systems because
child transaccións may be run concurrently in different servers. We return to this issue in Chapter 17. This form of transacciones anidadas is due to Moss [1985]. Other variants of
transacciones anidadas with different serializability properties have been proposed; for example, see Weikum [1991].

# 16.4 Bloqueos

16.4 Bloqueos
Transaccións must be scheduled so that their effect on shared data is serially equivalent.
A server can achieve serial equivalence of transaccións by serializin g access to the objects. Figura 16.7 shows an example of how serial equivalence can be achieved with
some de gree of concurrenc y – transaccións T and U both access account B, but T completes its access before U starts accessing it.
A simple example of a serializing mechanism is the use of exclusive bloqueos. In this bloqueo scheme, the server attempts to loc k any object that is about to be used by any
operation of a client's transacción. If a client requests access to an object that is already bloqueoed due to another client 's transacción, the request is suspended and the client must
wait until the object is unbloqueoed.
Figura 16.14 illustrates the use of exclusive bloqueos. It shows the same transaccións as Figura 16.7, but with an e xtra colu mn for each transacción showin g the loc king,
waiting and unloc king. In this example, it is assu med that when transaccións T and U start, the balances of the accounts A, B and C are not yet bloqueoed. When transacción T is
about to use account B, it is bloqueoed for T. When transacción U is about to use B it is still

whereupon transacción U is resumed. The use of the bloqueo on B effectively serializes the access to B. Note that if, for example, T released the bloqueo on B between its getBalance
and setBalance operations, transacción U's getBalance operation on B could be interleaved between them.
Serial equivalence requires that all of a transacción's accesses to a particular object be serializado with respect to accesses by other transaccións. All pairs of conflicting
operations of two transactio ns should be e xecuted in the same order. To ensure this, a transacción is not allowed an y new bloqueos after it has released a loc k. The first phase of

bloqueo.

Concurrency control protocols are desi gned to cope with conflicts between operations in different transaccións on the same object. In this chapter, we use the notion

Before a transacción 's read operation is performed, a read loc k should be set on the object. Before a transacción's write operation is performed, a write bloqueo should be set on
the object. Whenever it is impossible to set a bloqueo immediately, the transacción (and the client) must wait until it is possible to do so – a client's request is never rejected.
As pairs of read operations from different transaccións do not conflict, an attempt to set a read bloqueo on an object with a read bloqueo is always successful. All the transaccións

The operation conflict rules tell us that:
1. If a transacción T has alread y performed a read operation on a particular ob ject,
then a concurrent transacción U must not write that ob ject until T confirmars or abortars.
2. If a transacción T has already performed a write operation on a particular ob ject,
then a concurrent transacción U must not read or write that object until T confirmars or abortars.
To enforce condition 1, a request for a write bloqueo on an object is delayed by the presence of a read loc k belonging to another transacción. To enforce condition 2, a request for
either a read bloqueo or a write bloqueo on an object is delayed by the presence of a write bloqueo belonging to another transacción.

16.5 Control optimista de la concurrencia
Kung and Robinson [1981] identified a number of inherent disadvantages of bloqueo and proposed an alternative opti mistic approach to the serialization of transaccións that
avoids these drawbacks. We can summarize the drawbacks of bloqueo:
 Bloqueo maintenance represents an overhead that is not present in systems that do not support acceso concurrente to shared data. Even read-only transaccións (queries),
which cannot possibly affect the integrity of the data, must, in general, use bloqueo in order to guarantee that the data being read is not modified by other transaccións
at the same time. But bloqueo may be necessary only in the worst case.
For example, consider two client processes that are concurrently incrementing the values of n objects. If the client programs start at the same time and run for about
the same amount of ti me, accessing the objects in two unrelated sequences and using a separate transacción to access and incre ment each ite m, the chances that
the two programs will attempt to access the same object at the same time are just
1 in n on average, so bloqueo is really needed only once in every n transaccións.
 The use of bloqueos can result in deadbloqueo. Deadbloqueo prevention reduces concurrency severely, and therefore deadloc k situations must be resolved either by the use of
timeouts or by deadbloqueo detection. Neither of these is wholl y satisfactory for use in interactive programs.
 To avoid cascadin g abortars, loc ks cannot be released until the end of the transacción. This may reduce significantly the potential for concurrency.
The alternative approach proposed by Kung and Robinson is â€˜optimistic' because it is based on the observation that, in most applications, the li kelihood of two clients '
transaccións accessing the same object is low. Transaccións are allowed to proceed as though there were no possibilit y of conflict with other transaccións until the client
completes its task and issues a closeTransacción request. When a conflict arises, so me transacción is generally abortared and will need to be restarted by the client. Each
transacción has the following phases:
Working phase: During the fase de trabajo, each transacción has a tentative version of each of the objects that it updates. This is a cop y of the most recently confirmarted
version of the ob ject. The use of tentative versions allows the transacción to abortar
(with no effect on the objects), either during the fase de trabajo or if it fails validación due to other conflicting transaccións. read operations are performed immediately – if
a tentative version for that transacción alread y exists, a read operation accesses it;
otherwise, it accesses the most recentl y confirmarted value of the ob ject. write operations record the new values of the objects as tentative values (which are
invisible to other transaccións). When there are several concurrent transaccións,
several different tentative values of the same object may coe xist. In addition, two records are kept of the objects accessed within a transacción: a conjunto de lectura containing the
objects read by the transacción and a conjunto de escritura containing the objects written by the transacción. Note that as all read operations are performed on confirmarted versions of
the objects (or copies of them), dirty reads cannot occur.

461: 16.5 Control optimista de la concurrencia
462: Kung and Robinson [1981] identified a number of inherent disadvantages of bloqueo and proposed an alternative opti mistic approach to the serialization of transaccións that
463: avoids these drawbacks. We can summarize the drawbacks of bloqueo:
464:  Bloqueo maintenance represents an overhead that is not present in systems that do not support acceso concurrente to shared data. Even read-only transaccións (queries),
465: which cannot possibly affect the integrity of the data, must, in general, use bloqueo in order to guarantee that the data being read is not modified by other transaccións
466: at the same time. But bloqueo may be necessary only in the worst case.
467: For example, consider two client processes that are concurrently incrementing the values of n objects. If the client programs start at the same time and run for about
468: the same amount of ti me, accessing the objects in two unrelated sequences and using a separate transacción to access and incre ment each ite m, the chances that
469: the two programs will attempt to access the same object at the same time are just
470: 1 in n on average, so bloqueo is really needed only once in every n transaccións.
471:  The use of bloqueos can result in deadbloqueo. Deadbloqueo prevention reduces concurrency severely, and therefore deadloc k situations must be resolved either by the use of
472: timeouts or by deadbloqueo detection. Neither of these is wholl y satisfactory for use in interactive programs.
473:  To avoid cascadin g abortars, loc ks cannot be released until the end of the transacción. This may reduce significantly the potential for concurrency.

Las transacciones anidadas extienden el modelo de transacciones anterior permitiendo que las transacciones se compongan de otras transacciones. Así, varias transacciones pueden iniciarse desde dentro de una

La transacción más externa transacción en un conjunto de transacciones anidadas se denomina transacción de nivel superior. Las transacciones distintas de the transacción de nivel superior se denominan subtransacciones.

When we need to distinguish our original form of transacción fro m nested ones,
we use the term transacción plana. Es plana porque todo su trabajo se realiza al mismo nivel between an openTransacción and a confirmar or abortar, and it is not possible to confirmar or
abortar parts of it. Transacciones anidadas have the following main advantages:
1. Subtransaccións at one level (and their descendants) may run concurrently with other subtransacciones at the same level in the hierarchy. This can allow additional
concurrency in a transacción. When subtransacciones run in different servers, the y can work in parallel. For example, consider the branchTotal operation in our
banking example. It can be implemented by invoking getBalance at every account in the branch. Now each of these invocations may be performed as a
subtransacción, in which case they can be performed concurrently. Since each one applies to a different account, there will be no conflicting operations a mong the
subtransacciones.
2. Subtransaccións can confirmar or abortar independently. In comparison with a single transacción, a set of nested subtransacciones is potentially more robust. The above
example of delivering mail shows that this is so – with a transacción plana, one transacción failure would cause the whole transacción to be restarted. In fact, a
parent can decide on different actions accordin g to whether a subtransacción has abortared or not.
The rules for confirmarting of transacciones anidadas are rather subtle:
 A transacción may confirmar or abortar only after its child transaccións have completed.
 When a subtransacción completes, it makes an independent decision either to confirmar provisionally or to abortar. Its decision to abortar is final.
 When a parent abortars, all of its subtransacciones are abortared. For example, if T2 abortars then T21 and T211 must also abortar, even though they may have provisionally
confirmarted.
 Cuando una subtransacción aborta, the parent can decide whether to abortar or not. In our example, T decides to confirmar although T2 has abortared.

--- PAGE 710 --692
 If the transacción de nivel superior confirmars, then all of the subtransacciones that have provisionally confirmarted can confirmar too, provided that none of their ancestors has
abortared. In our example, T's confirmarment allows T1, T11 and T12 to confirmar, but not T21 and T211 since their parent, T2, abortared. Note that the effects of a
subtransacción are not permanent until the transacción de nivel superior confirmars.
In some cases, the transacción de nivel superior may decide to abortar because one or more of its subtransacciones have abortared. As an example, consider the following Transfer
transacción:
Transfer $100 from B to A a.deposit(100)
b.withdraw(100)
This can be structured as un par de subtransacciones, one for the withdraw operation and the other for deposit. When the two subtransacciones both confirmar, the Transfer
transacción can also confirmar. Suppose that a withdraw subtransacción abortars whenever an account is overdrawn. Now consider the case when the withdraw subtransacción
abortars and the deposit subtransacción confirmars – and recall that the confirmarment of a child transacción is conditional on la transacción padre confirmarting. We presume that
the nivel superior ( Transfer) transacción will decide to abortar. The abortaring of la transacción padre causes the subtransacciones to abortar – so the deposit transacción is abortared and
all its effects are undone.
The COR BA Ob ject Transacción Service supports both flat and transacciones anidadas. Transacciones anidadas are particularly useful in distributed systems because
child transaccións may be run concurrently in different servers. We return to this issue in Chapter 17. This form of transacciones anidadas is due to Moss [1985]. Other variants of
transacciones anidadas with different serializability properties have been proposed; for example, see Weikum [1991].

# 16.4 Bloqueos

16.4 Bloqueos
Transaccións must be scheduled so that their effect on shared data is serially equivalent.
A server can achieve serial equivalence of transaccións by serializin g access to the objects. Figura 16.7 shows an example of how serial equivalence can be achieved with
some de gree of concurrenc y – transaccións T and U both access account B, but T completes its access before U starts accessing it.
A simple example of a serializing mechanism is the use of exclusive bloqueos. In this bloqueo scheme, the server attempts to loc k any object that is about to be used by any
operation of a client's transacción. If a client requests access to an object that is already bloqueoed due to another client 's transacción, the request is suspended and the client must
wait until the object is unbloqueoed.
Figura 16.14 illustrates the use of exclusive bloqueos. It shows the same transaccións as Figura 16.7, but with an e xtra colu mn for each transacción showin g the loc king,
waiting and unloc king. In this example, it is assu med that when transaccións T and U start, the balances of the accounts A, B and C are not yet bloqueoed. When transacción T is
about to use account B, it is bloqueoed for T. When transacción U is about to use B it is still

whereupon transacción U is resumed. The use of the bloqueo on B effectively serializes the access to B. Note that if, for example, T released the bloqueo on B between its getBalance
and setBalance operations, transacción U's getBalance operation on B could be interleaved between them.
Serial equivalence requires that all of a transacción's accesses to a particular object be serializado with respect to accesses by other transaccións. All pairs of conflicting
operations of two transactio ns should be e xecuted in the same order. To ensure this, a transacción is not allowed an y new bloqueos after it has released a loc k. The first phase of
each transacción is a â€˜growing phase ', durin g which new loc ks are acquired. In the second phase, the loc ks are released (a â€˜shrinking phase '). This is called two-phase
bloqueo.
We saw in Section 16.2.2 that because transaccións may abortar, strict e xecutions are needed to prevent dirty reads and premature writes. Under a strict execution regime,
a transacción that needs to read or write an ob ject must be dela yed until other transaccións that wrote the same object have confirmarted or abortared. To enforce this rule,
any loc ks applied durin g the pro gress of a transacción are held until the transacción confirmars or abortars. This is called strict two-phase bloqueo . The presence of the loc ks
prevents other transaccións reading or writing the objects. When a transacción confirmars,
to ensure recoverability, the bloqueos must be held until all the objects it updated have been written to permanent storage.
A server generally contains a lar ge number of objects, and a t ypical transacción accesses only a few of them and is unlikely to clash with other current transaccións. The
granularity with which concurrenc y control can be applied to objects is an i mportant

--- PAGE 712 --694
issue, since the scope for acceso concurrente to objects in a server will be limited severely if concurrency control (for example, bloqueos) can only be applied to all the objects at once.
In our banking example, if bloqueos were applied to all customer accounts at a branch, only one ban k cler k could perfor m an online ban king transacción at an y ti me – hardl y an
acceptable constraint!
The portion of the objects to which access must be serializado should be as s mall as possible; that is, just that part involved in each operation requested by transaccións.
In our banking example, a branch holds a set of accounts, each of which has a balance.
Each banking operation affects one or more account balances – deposit and withdraw affect one account balance, and branchTotal affects all of them.
The description of concurrency control schemes given below does not assume any particular granularity. We discuss concurrenc y control protocols that are applicable to
objects whose operations can be modelled in terms of read and write operations on the objects. For the protocols to work correctl y, it is essential that each read and write
operation is atomic in its effects on objects.
Concurrency control protocols are desi gned to cope with conflicts between operations in different transaccións on the same object. In this chapter, we use the notion
of conflict between operations to e xplain the protocols. The conflict rules for read and write operations are given in Figura 16.9, which shows that pairs of read operations
from different transaccións on the same ob ject do not conflict. Therefore, a si mple exclusive bloqueo that is used for both read and write operations reduces concurrency more
than is necessary.
It is preferable to adopt a bloqueo scheme that controls the access to each object so that there can be several concurrent transaccións readin g an ob ject, or a sin gle
transacción writin g an ob ject, but not both. This is commonly referred to as a â€˜many readers/single writer' scheme. Two types of bloqueos are used: read bloqueos and write bloqueos.
Before a transacción 's read operation is performed, a read loc k should be set on the object. Before a transacción's write operation is performed, a write bloqueo should be set on
the object. Whenever it is impossible to set a bloqueo immediately, the transacción (and the client) must wait until it is possible to do so – a client's request is never rejected.
As pairs of read operations from different transaccións do not conflict, an attempt to set a read bloqueo on an object with a read bloqueo is always successful. All the transaccións
reading the same object share its read loc k – for this reason, read loc ks are sometimes called shared bloqueos.
The operation conflict rules tell us that:
1. If a transacción T has alread y performed a read operation on a particular ob ject,
then a concurrent transacción U must not write that ob ject until T confirmars or abortars.
2. If a transacción T has already performed a write operation on a particular ob ject,
then a concurrent transacción U must not read or write that object until T confirmars or abortars.
To enforce condition 1, a request for a write bloqueo on an object is delayed by the presence of a read loc k belonging to another transacción. To enforce condition 2, a request for
either a read bloqueo or a write bloqueo on an object is delayed by the presence of a write bloqueo belonging to another transacción.

writes the same object – when a subsequent transacción requires a read loc k it will be delayed until any current transacción has completed.
A transacción with a read loc k that is s hared with other transaccións cannot promote its read bloqueo to a write bloqueo, because the latter would conflict with the read bloqueos
held by the other transaccións. Therefore, such a transacción must request a write loc k and wait for the other read bloqueos to be released.
Bloqueo promotion refers to th e conversion of a bloqueo to a stron ger bloqueo – that is, a bloqueo that is more e xclusive. The loc k co mpatibility table in Figura 16.15 shows the
relative exclusivity of  loc ks. The read loc k allows other read bloqueos, whereas the write bloqueo does not. Neither allows other write bloqueos. Therefore, a write bloqueo is more exclusive
than a read bloqueo. Bloqueos may be promoted because the result is a more exclusive bloqueo. It is not safe to de mote a bloqueo held by a transacción before it confirmars, because the result
will be more per missive than the previous one and may allow e xecutions by other transaccións that are inconsistent with serial equivalence.
The rules for the use of loc ks in a stric t two-phase loc king implementation are summarized in Figura 16.16. To ensure that these rules are adhered to, the client has no

objects, and unbloqueo is performed by the confirmar or abortar operations of the transacción coordinator.

1.  When an operation accesses an object within a transacción:
(a)If the ob ject is not already bloqueoed, it is bloqueoed and the operation proceeds.
(b)If the ob ject has a conflicting bloqueo set by another transacción, the transacción must wait until it is unbloqueoed.

16.5 Control optimista de la concurrencia
Kung and Robinson [1981] identified a number of inherent disadvantages of bloqueo and proposed an alternative opti mistic approach to the serialization of transaccións that
avoids these drawbacks. We can summarize the drawbacks of bloqueo:
 Bloqueo maintenance represents an overhead that is not present in systems that do not support acceso concurrente to shared data. Even read-only transaccións (queries),
which cannot possibly affect the integrity of the data, must, in general, use bloqueo in order to guarantee that the data being read is not modified by other transaccións
at the same time. But bloqueo may be necessary only in the worst case.
For example, consider two client processes that are concurrently incrementing the values of n objects. If the client programs start at the same time and run for about
the same amount of ti me, accessing the objects in two unrelated sequences and using a separate transacción to access and incre ment each ite m, the chances that
the two programs will attempt to access the same object at the same time are just
1 in n on average, so bloqueo is really needed only once in every n transaccións.

timeouts or by deadbloqueo detection. Neither of these is wholl y satisfactory for use in interactive programs.

transaccións accessing the same object is low. Transaccións are allowed to proceed as though there were no possibilit y of conflict with other transaccións until the client

otherwise, it accesses the most recentl y confirmarted value of the ob ject. write operations record the new values of the objects as tentative values (which are
invisible to other transaccións). When there are several concurrent transaccións,
several different tentative values of the same object may coe xist. In addition, two records are kept of the objects accessed within a transacción: a conjunto de lectura containing the
objects read by the transacción and a conjunto de escritura containing the objects written by the transacción. Note that as all read operations are performed on confirmarted versions of
the objects (or copies of them), dirty reads cannot occur.
